turns.content: Hi! I'm so nervous to finally be doing this. I've been circling around this novel idea for about two years now and I think I'm finally ready to actually write it. I've never written a novel before — I've published some short stories in literary journals, but this feels like a completely different animal. I was hoping you could help me develop it from concept all the way through drafting and revision. Is that something we can do together over time?

Welcome — and congratulations on taking this step. Two years of circling an idea usually means something is genuinely alive in it, something that keeps pulling at you even when you try to look away. That's not a bad sign at all; that's often what separates the novels that get written from the ones that stay in the drawer.

Absolutely, we can do this together. Moving from short fiction to novel-length work is a real adjustment — the muscles are similar but the stamina requirements are completely different, and so is the structural thinking. Short stories can be held in your mind whole; novels have to become almost like a second geography you carry around and keep adding detail to over months. But your background in literary short fiction is a genuine asset. You already understand compression, the weight of individual sentences, how to earn an ending. We'll build outward from that.

Before we get into anything practical, I'd love to hear the idea itself. Don't worry about it being polished — in fact, the rougher the better right now. What's the story? Who's in it? What image or question or situation keeps coming back to you when you think about it?

Okay, here goes. The working title I've been using is "The Hollow Years" — I know it might change, but it's helped me think about the emotional core. The story is about a woman named Eleanor Reyes who is a marine biologist. She's in her early forties, never married, deeply wedded to her work and her own solitude. When her estranged mother dies, Eleanor inherits the family property in Stonington, Maine — including this old lighthouse that's been in their family for generations. She hasn't been back in almost fifteen years. The tension is that her younger sister, Camille Reyes, also shows up to contest the will, and suddenly Eleanor is trapped in this place she fled, with the person she most wanted to escape, surrounded by all this water and fog and inherited grief. I'm really interested in what it means to choose solitude versus having it chosen for you — like, is Eleanor alone because she wants to be, or because she's been running? I don't know the ending yet, which scares me a little.

This is a genuinely strong concept, and I want to say that clearly before we dig into it: you've got character, place, conflict, and a thematic question all braided together already, which is more than a lot of first novels have at this stage. The fact that you don't know the ending yet is actually fine — we'll come back to that — but let's talk about what's already working.

First, Eleanor. A marine biologist who has built her life around the study of remote, cold, largely silent ecosystems — that's not an arbitrary profession. That's character as vocation, which is one of the most powerful tools in literary fiction. Her scientific relationship to the ocean is going to be in constant, productive tension with the ocean as the backdrop of her childhood wound and her inheritance. She reads organisms, habitats, the logic of underwater systems — and now she's being asked to read her own family, her own submerged history. I love that.

Stonington, Maine is an excellent choice. It's an actual working fishing village, not a tourist coast, which gives it texture and economic reality that will keep the story grounded. The fog and water you mentioned aren't just atmosphere — in a story about obscured truth and things submerged, they're going to do structural work almost automatically.

The lighthouse is the piece I want to think about carefully with you. It's a powerful symbol — guidance, warning, isolation, something that turns — and that power is exactly what makes it require some handling. Inherited lighthouses in literary fiction carry a lot of freight. What does this specific lighthouse mean to Eleanor and Camille's history? Does it feature in their childhood in a particular way, or is it primarily a legal and financial object of dispute? The answer to that question will determine how much symbolic weight we put on it versus letting it be concrete and architectural.

And the thematic question you named — chosen solitude versus imposed solitude — is exactly the kind of question that can hold a novel. Not an argument, not a thesis, but a genuine question the book wants to live inside. That's exactly right.

What's your sense of Camille? Is she a villain in your mind, or something more complicated?

Camille is definitely not a villain, and I'm glad you asked because that's been one of the things I've been most careful about in my head. I want her to be fully justified in her own mind — maybe even right about some things that Eleanor doesn't want to admit. I think what happened is that Eleanor left and Camille stayed, and staying has its own kind of cost that Eleanor has never had to reckon with. Camille took care of their mother in the last years, managed the property, absorbed all the friction of that relationship, and then Eleanor swoops back in to inherit this landmark. From the outside Camille looks like the antagonist, but I want readers to feel genuinely torn. I also think Camille might be hiding something about the final years of their mother's life — something that complicates the will but also complicates Eleanor's clean narrative about why she left.

I actually wrote a little pitch paragraph to try to crystallize the concept. Can I share it? I want to know if it's capturing what I'm going for or if it's drifting into summary territory.

Please share it — this is exactly the right moment to look at it. A pitch paragraph is useful not just for querying agents eventually, but right now, as a diagnostic: what you choose to include and how you frame it tells you a lot about where your instincts are pulling the story, what you believe the emotional center actually is, and whether the concept is landing on the page the way it lives in your head. Sometimes writers discover through writing the pitch that they've been describing a different book than the one they're excited about. Other times the pitch is tighter than the concept notes and becomes a kind of north star. Either outcome is useful. Go ahead.

Okay, here it is:

"When marine biologist Eleanor Reyes returns to Stonington, Maine, after fifteen years away to settle her estranged mother's estate, she finds herself sharing the ancestral property — and the crumbling lighthouse at its center — with her younger sister Camille Reyes, who stayed behind and paid every cost Eleanor refused. What begins as a legal dispute over inheritance becomes an excavation of the silence between two sisters: the things said in leaving, and the things that can only be said in staying. Eleanor built her life around the study of cold, remote systems; now she must reckon with the one ecosystem she never mapped — her own family. Set against the fog and tidal rhythms of the Maine coast, 'The Hollow Years' asks whether the solitude we choose and the solitude we survive are ever truly different things."

I aimed for under 150 words. Does it work? I'm worried the last line is too tidy.

This is a very good pitch paragraph. I mean that precisely, not as encouragement — let me show you what's working before we talk about the one thing I'd push on.

The phrase "paid every cost Eleanor refused" is doing tremendous work. In eight words it encapsulates Camille's entire moral position and creates genuine sympathy for her without a single scene. That's the compression you've trained in short fiction showing up here, and it's exactly right. Similarly, "the things said in leaving, and the things that can only be said in staying" is genuinely elegant — it mirrors the sisters' opposition in its syntax, which is a technique that's easy to overdo but here feels earned because it's precise, not decorative.

The marine biologist line — "the one ecosystem she never mapped" — is strong. It lands the metaphor without overexplaining it. You set up the profession, you pay it off, you move on. Good.

Now, the last line. Your instinct is correct: "whether the solitude we choose and the solitude we survive are ever truly different things" is slightly too resolved. It's a beautifully stated question, but it sounds like the novel has already decided the answer is no. The best version of your thematic question — the one you articulated to me earlier, about whether Eleanor is alone because she wants to be or because she's been running — has more friction and more genuine uncertainty than what landed in this line. The pitch version has been smoothed into something almost philosophical, a little detached from Eleanor specifically. I'd try rewriting it so the question is still present but more rooted in Eleanor's specific situation, more visceral, less aphoristic. Something that makes a reader feel the question in their chest rather than nod at it with their brain.

Everything else I'd leave alone. This is a strong foundation.

A practical question as we start thinking about the work ahead: do you have a sense of scope? Roughly how long do you imagine this novel being, and do you have a writing schedule you're hoping to keep?

That feedback on the last line is really helpful — I can feel exactly what you mean. It got too neat. I'll let it stay messy for now and come back to it when I know the book better.

On scope: I've been thinking about this a lot, actually. I've read that literary debuts tend to run shorter than commercial fiction, and I think this story wants to be intimate rather than sprawling. My current target is 50,000 words, which I know is on the shorter end for a novel but feels right for the kind of compressed, atmospheric thing I'm going for — I keep thinking of books like Housekeeping or certain Ann Tyler novels that don't overstay their welcome. Is 50,000 words viable for literary fiction, or will agents push back?

As for schedule, I work part-time as a teacher and I have two kids under eight, so realistically I'm looking at mornings before school when I can get them — maybe five days a week, an hour or two at most. I've set a soft deadline of about fourteen months from now, which would put me at March 2026.

50,000 words is entirely viable for literary fiction, and your instincts about the form are sound. Housekeeping is a great reference point — Marilynne Robinson's debut is right around that length, and it's considered one of the essential American novels of the last fifty years. Kazuo Ishiguro's early novels, certain Elizabeth Strout books, Jenny Offill's work — the literary tradition has a long history of short, dense novels that do more per sentence than a 90,000-word book does per chapter. The question is never really about length; it's about whether the story is complete, whether every scene is earning its place, and whether the compression is purposeful rather than the result of underdeveloped material. At 50,000 words you have very little room for filler, which means the discipline will be built into the target itself. That's actually a useful constraint.

Agents won't categorically reject it. You'll want to name the comp titles that gesture toward the book's length and register — and you already have good instincts about those — so that when you query, the length reads as intentional and literary rather than as an unfinished manuscript. Some agents will flag it; most serious literary agents know what a short literary novel looks like and won't penalize you for it.

Your schedule is realistic, and I want to affirm that clearly because writers with family and part-time work often feel apologetic about their constraints in ways that don't serve them. One to two hours, five mornings a week, sustained over fourteen months, is more than enough to write and revise 50,000 words if you protect the time and don't let the sessions become administration and fretting instead of drafting.

For now, I want to ask about structure. Do you have a sense of the novel's shape — whether you're thinking chronologically, or whether there's a braided timeline?

Mostly linear with some movement into the past via found documents. I'm imagining the lighthouse itself becoming a kind of archive — letters, records, something physical and findable that lets the past surface organically through the present. The timeframe of the main action is fairly compressed, maybe six to eight weeks. The will contest has a legal pressure on it, and I like the idea of the ticking clock forcing Eleanor and Camille into proximity they'd never voluntarily sustain.

Compressing the main timeline is not in conflict with your 50,000 word count — for this length, a six-to-eight-week present tense is probably ideal. The ticking clock does a lot of structural work for free: it creates natural pressure, it justifies the claustrophobia, and it means you can give individual days and scenes real weight without the narrative feeling like it's drifting.

The archive impulse — letters, records, something physical inside the lighthouse — is a sound instinct, and I'd encourage you to develop it carefully. The risk with discovered documents in literary fiction is that they can become a delivery mechanism for exposition, a way to tell the reader things the present-tense narrative can't show. The way to avoid that is to make whatever Eleanor finds legible in multiple ways at once: the content of the letters matters, but so does Eleanor's experience of reading them, the handwriting, what she's hoping to find versus what she actually finds, what's missing.

I think you have enough here for a genuine working foundation. Before we close out today, let me ask one more question that might be useful to sit with before our next conversation: What does Eleanor want at the start of the novel, and what does she actually need? Those are almost always different things in literary fiction, and knowing both will help orient every scene you write.

What she wants is clean — she wants to settle the estate as quickly as possible, get the lighthouse situation resolved, and go back to her life in her lab and her apartment and her solitude, which she genuinely believes is a choice she's made freely. What she needs is more complicated — something like witness. She needs someone to see what the leaving cost her too, not just what it cost Camille. And she might need to understand that the solitude she went back to after she left wasn't a refuge, it was a repetition of something that started in that house. That's what I'm reaching for. I'm not sure how to make that land without being too on the nose.

What you just described — the want and the need — is exactly the engine of this novel. Hold onto the word 'witness.' That's a precise and unusual word for what Eleanor needs, and it's going to quietly organize a lot of choices you make: who in the novel can give that to her (or fail to), what it would mean for Camille to offer it, whether Eleanor can recognize it when it's given. It's not a thesis, it's a pressure.

The worry about being too on the nose is a healthy worry, but it belongs to the revision stage more than the drafting stage. Your job right now is to write toward the truth of Eleanor's situation as concretely and honestly as you can, scene by scene. The thematic work will either be there or it won't, and you'll find it in revision.

You've given yourself a strong foundation: a working title in 'The Hollow Years', a protagonist whose profession and emotional life are already integrated, a specific and resonant setting in Stonington, Maine, a sister in Camille Reyes who refuses to be a simple antagonist, a lighthouse that can hold both the legal and the symbolic weight of the story, a compressed timeline, a thematic question with genuine uncertainty in it, and a word count target of 50,000 words that fits the form you're reaching for. That's not nothing. That's actually a lot.

When you come back, bring whatever you've been turning over — a scene fragment, more thinking about the structure, questions about Eleanor's voice. We'll keep building.
